metadata.note: deep-explainer, fresh technical build comparing Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector, Qdrant, Chroma across 6 required points: indexing algorithm/strategy, pre/post filtering, multitenancy, scalability, production drawbacks, use cases. 4 acts: I indexing+filtering, II multitenancy+scalability, III drawbacks, IV use cases. Content is general, well-established, publicly-documented architecture (HNSW/IVF, managed-vs-self-hosted, Postgres-extension model) -- deliberately hedged away from version-specific or benchmark-number claims per DOUBLE-CHECK LAW (see FACTCHECK.md). No Manim on this machine (pangocairo not installed) -- MANIM lane absorbed into REMOTION. VOX quota: 5 real Wikimedia Commons photographs, metaphor imagery. BinaryBranch/DivergentFates hero beats planned up front at A1-5, A2-3, A2-5, A3-4, A4-3 (one per act, two in Act II) for clean 9:16 Short derivation. Signed for Divyank (not Nik Bear Brown) from authoring time -- folderLabel/handle/sign-off all use @DivyankSingh / 'in for Divyank' throughout. GATE P: PENDING, see PEDAGOGY.md.

beats.narration_text: Jambo — this is Liam, in for Divyank. Five real databases all claim to do the same thing: find the nearest vectors, fast. They don't do it the same way, and the differences are exactly where production systems break. Let's take all five apart, side by side.

send arms, runningText plays
RESULT lines land in sequence

props.command: Compare Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector, Qdrant, and Chroma — indexing, filtering, multitenancy, scalability, drawbacks, and use cases.
output: they don't index the same way
filtering strategy decides whether metadata queries actually work
no universal winner — five different bets

beats.act: Act I — How Each One Finds Your Vector
beats.narration_text: Underneath every one of these databases is the same problem a subway map solves: don't search every station. Follow a small number of well-chosen connections straight to the one you actually need.

shot.prompt: real archival subway-map photo -- illustrative of an index as a fast-navigation map, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A1-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push into the map's line network
serif label lands: 'a map, not a search of everything'

beats.act: Act I — How Each One Finds Your Vector
beats.narration_text: Try a highly selective filter — one percent of your data — against a naive post-filter implementation. Search for the top ten neighbors, and every single one of them can fail the filter. Zero results, from a database that has the right answer sitting right there.

show.event: question card: 'filter matches 1% of the data — then what?'
two outcomes: naive post-filter / integrated pre-filter

data.question: A filter matches 1% of your data — then what?

branches.label: Naive post-filter
branches.detail: top-10 neighbors, all fail the filter

resolver.label: The strategy decides, not the algorithm
resolver.detail: same data, same query, different answer

beats.act: Act II — Who Else Is In Your Index
beats.narration_text: One building, many separate units, one shared foundation. That's the multitenancy question for a vector database: how many customers' data can share one index without ever leaking into each other's search results.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of a building with many windows -- illustrative of multitenancy, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A2-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push up the building
serif label lands: 'many units, one shared foundation'

beats.act: Act II — Who Else Is In Your Index
beats.narration_text: One shared index with a tenant filter on every query, or one index per tenant. Shared scales cheaper and isolates worse under a filtering bug. One-per-tenant isolates perfectly and gets expensive fast — thousands of tenants means thousands of indexes to keep warm.

show.event: question card: 'one shared index, or one per tenant?'
two outcomes: shared / per-tenant

data.question: One shared index, or one per tenant?

branches.label: Shared index + filter
branches.fix: a filtering bug leaks across tenants

branches.label: One index per tenant
branches.fix: thousands of tenants, thousands of warm indexes

resolver.label: Every one of the five picks a lane
resolver.detail: there's no free version of this decision

beats.act: Act II — Who Else Is In Your Index
beats.narration_text: Same requirement — billions of vectors — two different ceilings. Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant scale outward: shard the index, add nodes, keep growing. Pgvector scales the way Postgres scales — mostly vertically, on one instance, with read replicas doing the rest.

show.event: two tracks diverge: horizontal scale-out arcs up good, Postgres vertical ceiling arcs down warn

tracks.label: Pinecone / Weaviate / Qdrant
tracks.outcome: shard and add nodes — keeps growing
notes: built to be sharded from day one

tracks.label: pgvector
tracks.outcome: mostly vertical, on one Postgres instance
notes: read replicas help, don't remove the ceiling

beats.act: Act III — What Breaks in Production
beats.narration_text: Every one of these five carries a real structural tradeoff — the kind you only feel once you're actually under load.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of steel beams stabilizing a bridge -- illustrative of production tradeoffs, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A3-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push along the beams
serif label lands: 'felt only under load'

beats.act: Act III — What Breaks in Production
beats.narration_text: Managed removes the operational burden and adds vendor lock-in. Self-hosted removes the lock-in and hands the operational burden right back to your team. Every one of these five picks a side — none of them gets both for free.

show.event: question card: 'managed, or self-hosted?'
two outcomes: managed / self-hosted

data.slideMeta: the operational fork behind most drawbacks
data.question: Managed, or self-hosted?

branches.label: Self-hosted
branches.fix: the ops burden is now yours

resolver.label: Nobody gets both for free
resolver.detail: the umbrella pattern behind most of these drawbacks

beats.narration_text: Five real tools, five real jobs. The wrong question is which one is best. The right one is which job you actually have.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of an organized tool case -- illustrative of picking the right tool for the job, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A4-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push into the compartments
serif label lands: 'which job you actually have'

beats.narration_text: Already running Postgres in production? Pgvector removes an entire system from your stack, for a real cost in scaling ceiling. Starting from zero? A dedicated engine costs you one more system to run, in exchange for a ceiling you won't hit for years.

show.event: question card: 'already on Postgres?'
two outcomes: yes / starting from zero

branches.label: Yes
branches.detail: pgvector removes a whole system from the stack

branches.label: Starting from zero
branches.detail: a dedicated engine is one more system to run
branches.fix: buys a ceiling you won't hit for years

resolver.label: Both are legal answers
resolver.detail: the question decides which, not a leaderboard
